The DOORS are attested reading-traditions surfaced from the retrieved reception store (~/reception-corpus), NOT authored from recall; every witness `reading` is the source's own words, lightly trimmed (Glossa editorial source-markers like ((AUG.)) dropped). The editorial framing (trap/hinge/gravity/synthesis/claim/say/do/subtract) is AI-drafted and pending Wilson's curation. [Authored 2026-10-06, Opus, Phase 4b brief, born v2: Gospel doors from the Catena Aurea (Newman tr.) rows on Matt 25:1-13 via src/turn_sources.py, plus Glossa ordinaria (Migne) 25:5 and 25:9, Wesley's Notes 25:3/25:4/25:5/25:8/25:9/25:13, and the Catena intertext echo of Habakkuk 2:3; both tracks authored from src/turn_pull.py output. Semicontinuous: three Joshua 24 doors (Wesley 24:2-3, 24:14-15, 24:19-22; Migne 24:19; Catena intertext at Matt 6:24 and Luke 1:67-75); the reading is split (24:1-3a, 14-25), so refKeys carries both spans. Migne's Joshua 24 glosses are Augustine incipit-excipit pointers ('etc., as far as'); only 24:19 was used, with the omission marked by an ellipsis, and 24:3/24:23 were left out. Complementary: Wisdom 6:12-16 has no Wesley rows (Apocrypha) and only three Migne glosses, so it carries two doors on Migne alone; the Migne glosses are keyed to Vulgate verse numbers (its 6:12 'Love them … and you shall have discipline' falls just before the English pericope). The lone Catena intertext on Wis 6:12-16 (Col 1:28, low, contested) was not used; the Wis 6:17-20 'psalm' rows (sorites taken up at 2 Peter 1) inform gravity/synthesis only. Psalm 78 rows likewise inform the semicontinuous gravity/synthesis only.]
trap: The parable becomes a scold about being prepared — a spiritual fire drill in which the wise are the organized people and the sermon is a to-do list — and the five who share nothing sound like the pastor's model for selfish piety. Or it slides into end-times arithmetic about when the bridegroom will come, and nobody notices that everyone in the story, wise and foolish alike, fell asleep.
hinge: All ten took lamps, all ten went out to meet him, all ten slept — and the only difference is oil no one can see until midnight and no one can lend once the cry goes up. The wise refuse to share, and the door is shut on people who knock calling him Lord. The parable will not let readiness be borrowed, and will not let it be postponed.

doors.claim: The bridegroom is late and everyone sleeps; the wise are not the ones who stay awake but the ones whose lamps are still supplied when the cry comes — a quiet heart that has not stopped waiting.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: While the bridegroom delayed — That is, before they were called to attend him, they all slumbered and slept - Were easy and quiet, the wise enjoying a true, the foolish a false peace.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Watch therefore — He that watches has not only a burning lamp, but likewise oil in his vessel. And even when he sleepeth, his heart waketh. He is quiet; but not secure.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: And the bridegroom tarrying. Because there is no little time between the first and the second coming of Christ. They all slumbered and slept. Because they are afterwards to be raised up.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: Whilst the bridegroom tarried, and the Word comes not speedily to the consummation of this life, the senses suffer, slumbering and moving in the night of the world. Yet did those wise virgins not quit their lamps, nor despair of hoarding their oil.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'Though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not delay' frames the theme of the bridegroom's delay (v.5) and the call to keep ready through the apparent postponement of the appointed time. (Echo of Habakkuk 2:3)

doors.say: Everybody in this story falls asleep — even the wise. The question is not whether you got tired of waiting; it's whether there's still oil in the jar when he comes.
doors.do: Ask them to name the long wait they are in — for healing, for justice, for Christ's coming — and to keep one small daily practice that refills the lamp while they wait.

doors.claim: At midnight no one can stand surety for anyone else: the wise do not refuse out of meanness but because holiness cannot be lent, and each must answer for their own lamp.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Give us of your oil, for our lamps are gone out — Our faith is dead. What a time to discover this! Unto which of the saints wilt thou then turn? Who can help thee at such a season?

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Lest there be not enough — It is sure there is not; for no man has more than holiness enough for himself.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Lest perhaps. Because each shall render an account for himself, nor is anyone helped before God by another's testimony, since to him secret things lie open, and each scarcely suffices for himself, that his own conscience may bear him witness.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Hence we learn that none of us shall be able in that day to stand forth as patron of those who are betrayed by their own works, not because he will not, but because he cannot.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: For these wise virgins do not answer thus out of covetousness, but out of fear. Wherefore, each man shall receive the recompense of his own works, and the virtues of one cannot atone for the vices of another in the day of judgment.

doors.say: You can borrow a great deal from the church — its prayers, its creeds, its saints. You cannot borrow its faith at midnight. Somebody else's oil will not light your lamp.
doors.do: Invite them to ask honestly whose oil they have been running on — a parent's faith, a spouse's, a congregation's — and to begin, this week, a practice of prayer that is their own.

doors.claim: The lamp is faith and the oil is love; the place to get it is among those who need mercy, and the time to buy is now, while the market is open.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The foolish took no oil with them — No more than kept them burning just for the present. The lamp is faith. A lamp and oil with it, is faith working by love.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The wise took oil in their vessels — Love in their hearts. And they daily sought a fresh supply of spiritual strength, till their faith was made perfect.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: It is to be observed, that all have lamps, but all have not oil.

witnesses.author: Hilary of Poitiers
witnesses.reading: They that sell are the poor, who, needing the alms of the faithful, made them that recompense which they desire, selling in return for the relief afforded to their wants, a consciousness of good works. This is the abundant fuel of an undying light which may be bought and stored up for the fruits of mercy.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: You see then how great merchants the poor are to us; but the poor are not there, but here, and therefore we must store up oil here, that we may have it to use there when occasion shall require.

doors.say: Everybody here has a lamp — you believe. The question is oil, and the Fathers say plainly where it's sold: in the hands of the poor, and only on this side of midnight.
doors.do: Name one concrete act of mercy toward someone in need that each listener can do before next Sunday — and call it buying oil.

doors.landing: She is waiting at your gate
doors.claim: Wisdom is not a prize hoarded for the clever: she runs ahead to meet those who desire her and sits at their door, offering herself freely — and the church has heard Christ knocking in her.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: She preventeth them that covet her. Offering herself freely. For he himself is the way, the truth, and the life: through him one goes, unto him one strives, to him one attains.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Her sitting by, etc. Ever ready, that is, to help, whence: Behold, I stand at the door and knock, if any man shall open to me, I will go in to him and will sup with him, and he with me.

doors.say: Wisdom is not off in a library waiting for you to earn her. She is sitting on your front step at dawn — and her name is Jesus.
doors.do: Ask them to rise early one morning this week, open the door of the day with Scripture before the phone, and see who is sitting there.

doors.landing: Love her, and keep her discipline
doors.claim: To desire Wisdom is to be formed by her: no one loves wisdom who will not keep her discipline, as no one loves Christ who will not keep his commandments.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Love them, etc., and you shall have discipline. He that loves wisdom keeps discipline in his manners. For he does not love wisdom who does not keep discipline. Whence: If you love me, keep my commandments.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: In the present life wisdom must be studied, and life led according to the rule of her discipline.

doors.say: Wanting wisdom and living by it are the same act. The wise virgins didn't just love the bridegroom — they bought oil.
doors.do: Have them choose one rule of life — a daily prayer, a fast, a Sabbath hour — and keep it as a way of loving Wisdom rather than earning her.

complementary.gravity: Wisdom is radiant and unfading, easily seen by those who love her; she goes out to meet those who desire her, sits at the gate of the one who rises early, and meets them in every thought (Wisdom 6:12-16). Desire for instruction becomes love, love becomes keeping her laws, and that leads to incorruption and a kingdom (Wisdom 6:17-20). Paul tells grieving Thessalonians the dead in Christ will rise and all will go out to meet the Lord; and five wise virgins go out to meet the bridegroom with oil while five foolish ones are left knocking. The nerve: wisdom is near and freely offered, and it still has to be wanted and kept.

synthesis.convergence: Wisdom runs to meet those who seek her and waits at their gate (Wisdom 6:12-16); desire for her climbs from instruction to love to obedience to a kingdom (Wisdom 6:17-20); the Thessalonians are told they will go out to meet the Lord with those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4); and the wise go out to meet the bridegroom with lamps supplied (Matthew 25). Each reading pictures a meeting — Wisdom coming to us, we going out to him — and the readiness that the meeting asks.
synthesis.claim: The one you are waiting for is already coming to meet you; wisdom is to want him enough to keep your lamp supplied.
synthesis.here: For people who think wisdom is a talent some have and others lack, the move is to hear that she is freely offered at their own door — and that the foolish virgins were not stupid, only unwilling to buy oil before they needed it.

doors.landing: Before you chose, you were taken
doors.claim: The covenant story starts with an idolater on the far side of the river whom God snatched out and led; whatever good is in the fathers was grace, so the choice Israel makes is an answer, not a beginning.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: They served - That is, Both Abraham and Nahor were no less idolaters than the rest of mankind. This is said to prevent their vain boasting in their worthy ancestors, and to assure them that whatsoever good was in, or had been done by their progenitors, was wholly from God's free grace, and not for their own merit or righteousness.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: I took — I snatched him out of that idolatrous place, and took him into acquaintance and covenant with myself, which was the highest honour and happiness he was capable of.

doors.say: Before Joshua asks the people to choose, God reminds them that Abraham was an idolater when God took him by the hand. Your yes to God is always a second word.
doors.do: Ask them to trace back where God took hold of them before they ever chose him — and to make this week's commitment as thanks, not as qualification.

doors.landing: As for me and my house
doors.claim: Joshua sets the choice before them because the service of God is so plainly better that anyone in their right mind would choose it — and declares he will choose it whatever the crowd does.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Choose ye - it is a powerful insinuation, whereby he both implies, that the worship of God is so highly reasonable, necessary and beneficial; and the service of idols so absurd, and vain, and pernicious, that if it were left free for all men to take their choice, every man in his right wits must needs chuse the service of God. They that resolve to serve God, must not start at being singular in it. They that are bound for heaven must be willing to swim against the stream, and must do, not as most do, but as the best do.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The gods — Whereby it appears, that although Joshua had doubtless prevented and purged out all public idolatry, yet there were some of them who practiced it in their private houses and retirements.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'Choose this day whom you will serve' — the exclusive either/or of covenant allegiance behind 'no one can serve two masters.' (taken up at Matthew 6:24)

doors.say: The idols Joshua worries about aren't in the public square; they're in the back rooms of people's houses. Choosing the Lord means choosing him there — even if you're the only house on the street.
doors.do: Invite each household to name one 'god in the back room' — a loyalty kept quietly beside the Lord — and to put it away together this week.

doors.claim: Joshua answers their eager yes with a no: God is holy and jealous, and their own promise will witness against them — not to discourage them, but so they will know the weight of what they vow, and need grace to keep it.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Ye cannot — He speaks not of an absolute impossibility, but of a moral impossibility, or a very great difficulty, which he alledgeth not to discourage them from God's service, but to make them more considerate in obliging themselves; and more resolved in answering their obligations. God's service is not, as you seem to fancy, a slight and easy thing, but it is a work of great difficulty, and requires great care, and courage and resolution.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Against yourselves — This solemn profession will be a swift witness against you, if hereafter you apostatize from God.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: You shall not be able. You shall not be able to serve the Lord … and afterwards grace might more abound through Jesus Christ, who is the end of the law.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'That we... should serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness' echoes the covenant summons to 'serve the Lord in sincerity and in faithfulness' (Joshua 24:14). (taken up at Luke 1:67-75)

doors.say: Joshua does what no recruiter would: he tells the people they can't do this. Only people who know they can't keep the covenant on their own will lean on the God who keeps it for them.
doors.do: Before any vow or recommitment, have them say aloud the hard part — what it will cost — and then ask for grace to keep it.

semicontinuous.gravity: At Shechem, the old leader gathers the tribes and tells the story from the top — your fathers served other gods beyond the river, and I took Abraham — then sets the choice before them: put away the gods, choose this day whom you will serve; as for me and my house. They shout yes, and Joshua says, you cannot; they say yes again, and he writes it down as a witness against them (Joshua 24). The Psalm commands the fathers to tell the next generation, so that children yet unborn would set their hope in God and not forget his works (Psalm 78). Paul says the dead in Christ are not lost; and Jesus tells of ten waiting for a bridegroom, some with oil and some without. The nerve: the covenant is renewed by each generation's own yes, and no one can make that choice — or carry that oil — for someone else.

synthesis.convergence: Joshua retells God's grace and sets a choice before every household, warning that the yes will cost them (Joshua 24); the Psalm charges each generation to tell the next so their children set their hope in God (Psalm 78); Paul comforts a church about those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4); and the bridegroom finds some ready and some not, with no oil to borrow (Matthew 25). Each reading turns on a faith that can be handed down but must be taken up by each one in their own time.
synthesis.claim: You can be told the story, but you have to choose the Lord yourself — and keep choosing him until he comes.
synthesis.here: For a congregation proud of its heritage and anxious about its children, the move is Joshua's: tell the whole story of grace, then put the choice to this generation plainly, without pretending it is easy and without pretending someone else's faith will carry them.

subtract: These three are doors, not points — mutually exclusive landings (patient waiting through the delay / no one else's oil / mercy as the oil). Walk through one and let the other two go; the choosing is the sermon's focus.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), and the Catena intertextual notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
